vesuvio.option.leafCulling.tooltip: Skips the leaf faces buried inside a canopy, which you cannot see but the GPU still draws (also in Etna's shadow pass). Only matters with cutout (fancy) leaves on. 0 = off, same as vanilla. 1 = smart (default): drops a face only when the next three blocks that way are leaves; about half of a forest's leaf faces go, and only about 1 in 50 canopy pixels shows sky where vanilla showed leaves. 2 = aggressive: two blocks are enough, like OptiFine's Smart Leaves; about two thirds go, canopies look a bit thinner (about 1 in 20 pixels). 3 = all: every face between two leaves goes; trees look hollow. Applies at once (the world's chunks are rebuilt), no restart.
vesuvio.screen.title: Vesuvio
vesuvio.screen.reset.tooltip: Puts every option on this page back to its default.
vesuvio.screen.masterOff: Off: the game runs as vanilla
vesuvio.screen.restartDue: Restart the game to apply the options marked *
vesuvio.screen.emptyPage: No options on this page yet.
vesuvio.screen.hint: Point at an option to see what it does. Every change applies at once and is saved; options marked * apply after a restart.
vesuvio.option.enabled.tooltip: The master switch. Off, every Vesuvio optimization stops at once and the game runs exactly as vanilla. Also on the F8 key (change it in Controls). No restart needed.
vesuvio.option.statsLog.tooltip: Writes fps and Vesuvio's live counters (what each optimization skipped) to latest.log every 5 seconds, for checking or sharing. Costs nothing visible. No restart needed.
vesuvio.option.benchmarkSeconds.tooltip: How many seconds the benchmark measures each step, after at least 3 seconds to settle (more while the world's chunks are being rebuilt). Longer is steadier but the run takes longer.
vesuvio.memory.title: Memory check
vesuvio.memory.advice.measuring: Play for two minutes in a world and Vesuvio will know how much memory the game really needs.
vesuvio.memory.advice.ok: The maximum of %s is fine. For this computer anything in %s works the same: more memory does not make the game faster.
vesuvio.memory.advice.low: The game needs about %s and may use at most %s, so it keeps cleaning up memory, which stutters. Raise the maximum to %s.
vesuvio.memory.advice.high: The game may use up to %s of this computer's %s, which leaves too little for the system and the graphics, so it may start swapping and stutter. Lower the maximum to %s.
vesuvio.memory.howTo: The maximum is set in the launcher, before the game starts. Prism Launcher: right-click the instance > Edit > Settings > Java > Maximum memory allocation. Official launcher: Installations > Edit > More options > JVM arguments, -Xmx4G for 4 GB. Click this button to see the advice in chat.
vesuvio.benchmark.tooltip: Measures fps with Vesuvio off, on, and with each optimization changed in turn (each setting on the other pages that needs no restart: a switch is flipped, a number such as Leaf Culling goes to 0), then on and off again. Stand still somewhere typical and don't touch anything: any key, click, move or menu stops it and puts your settings back. The results show at the end and go to latest.log.
vesuvio.benchmark.noWorld: Join a world first: the benchmark measures the game as you play it.
vesuvio.benchmark.started: Vesuvio benchmark: %s steps, about %s s. Stand still and don't touch anything; any key stops it.
vesuvio.benchmark.progress: Vesuvio benchmark %s/%s, %s left. Don't touch anything.
vesuvio.benchmark.partial: Stopped early: %s of %s steps measured, shown here and in latest.log.
vesuvio.benchmark.stopped: Vesuvio benchmark stopped (%s); settings put back.
vesuvio.benchmark.stop.input: a key or button was pressed
vesuvio.benchmark.done: Vesuvio benchmark done: off %s fps, on %s fps (%s%%). Table in latest.log.
vesuvio.benchmark.title: Vesuvio benchmark
vesuvio.benchmark.footer: vs on: ms per frame compared with Vesuvio on; + means what the step switched off was saving time.
vesuvio.option.memoryLightThreadChecks.t: Chunk data uses a tiny built-in check instead of a lock set (about 128 bytes) in every chunk section, and in every copy made to build or save one. Saves roughly 10 MB at render distance 12 and 50 MB at 32, with less garbage while chunks load. Still crashes with the same clear report if a mod misuses chunk data from two threads. No visual change. Needs a restart.
vesuvio.option.memoryShareBlockShapes.to: Blocks with identical shapes (walls, fences, panes, bars, fire, redstone...) share one shape object instead of thousands of copies, and walls/fences/panes reuse the shapes of the first block of their kind instead of computing them again. Saves roughly 10 MB and a little start-up time. No visual or gameplay change. Needs a restart.
vesuvio.option.memoryShareStateTables.to: Block states with the same face-support and face-occlusion tables share one table. Saves about 1.5 MB. No visual or gameplay change. Needs a restart.
vesuvio.option.memoryShareIdNamespaces.t: Ids read from game files and the network ("minecraft:stone") share one "minecraft" text instead of each keeping a copy. Saves about 1 MB. No visual or gameplay change. Needs a restart.
vesuvio.option.faceCulling.tooltip: Skips the faces of terrain that point away from you before the graphics card works on them (it would throw them away later anyway), saving about half the vertex work of the terrain. The picture does not change. Live: sections built while it was off are rebuilt in the background over a few seconds.
vesuvio.option.faceCullingMinGap.tooltip: How many hidden faces in the middle of a section are worth one extra draw call to skip, when the graphics card's time is what counts. Lower skips more faces but adds draw calls (CPU time); higher keeps draws down. Hidden faces at either end of a section are always skipped for free. On the Mac with Smart Splits on, it applies only while the graphics card is the limit. No look change, live.
vesuvio.option.faceCullingAutoSplit.tool: macOS only: splits a section's draw to skip hidden faces in its middle only while the graphics card is the limit (Vesuvio measures it every second: the game waits for the graphics card at least 10% of the frame). While the CPU is the limit no draw is split: on the Mac each extra draw costs CPU time and the work it saves lands on a graphics card that is waiting anyway. Hidden faces at either end are still skipped. Off: Split From always applies as set. Same picture either way, live. Does nothing on Windows and Linux.
vesuvio.option.sectionDrawCache.tooltip: The list of terrain draws for what you see is rebuilt only when something it depends on changed: which sections are visible, their meshes, where they sit in graphics memory, a section fading in, or you crossing a face culling boundary. Otherwise last frame's list is used again. Saves CPU time and garbage every frame, mostly when standing or looking around slowly. Same picture. Live.
vesuvio.option.skipRedundantBinds.toolti: In each render pass, does not bind again the shader pipeline that is already bound, and does not build a new set of textures and buffers for a draw when the set already bound holds exactly the same ones. Entities, particles and the menus repeat these for every single draw. Saves CPU time per draw (most on the Mac, where MoltenVK turns each one into Metal work). Same picture. Live.
vesuvio.option.fogCulling.tooltip: Skips terrain, mobs, block entities and particles so deep in the fog that they would be drawn in the plain fog colour anyway: under water, in lava or powder snow, with Blindness or Darkness, in the Nether and in a boss's fog. Uses the game's own fog distance of each frame, so nothing you could see disappears (in the open air the fog ends past the render distance and nothing is skipped). Turns itself off with Improved Transparency, near the world border, with debug overlays and while Etna Shaders draws the world. No restart.
vesuvio.option.entityCulling.tooltip: Skips drawing mobs, animals, item frames, dropped items and other entities hidden behind solid blocks (checked on a background thread). Looks the same, but an entity coming out from behind a wall can appear a frame late. Entities with a glowing outline, a visible name tag, a lead, or that you ride are always drawn. Works right away, no restart.
vesuvio.option.blockEntityCulling.toolti: Skips drawing chests, signs, banners, shulker boxes, skulls and other block entities that are outside your view or hidden behind solid blocks. Beacon beams, end gateways and structure blocks are always drawn. Looks the same, but one coming into view from behind a wall can appear a frame late. Works right away, no restart.
vesuvio.option.particleCulling.tooltip: Skips particles in places the game already knows you cannot see (the same check that hides caves and rooms behind walls). Particles outside your view are already skipped by the game. No change in look. Works right away, no restart.
vesuvio.option.signTextCulling.tooltip: Skips the text on the side of a sign that faces away from you (the graphics card would throw it away anyway), and all of a sign's text once each letter is smaller than one pixel at your window size and field of view. No change in look. No restart.
vesuvio.option.itemFrameCulling.tooltip: Skips item frames (with their item or map) when you are behind the wall they hang on and every block of that wall in the way is solid, and the framed item or map alone once it is smaller than one pixel. No change in look. No restart.
vesuvio.option.beaconBeamCulling.tooltip: The game draws every beacon beam every frame, even behind you. Skips beams wholly outside your view (with room for view bobbing and the tilt when hurt). No change in look. No restart.
vesuvio.option.animatedTextures.tooltip: Animated block textures (water, lava, fire, portals, sea lanterns...) are only redrawn while something on screen uses them. Saves GPU work on every texture tick. No change in look: a texture that comes into view starts moving again within one tick (1/20 s). Takes full effect for chunks built after it is switched on. No restart.
vesuvio.option.idleFps.tooltip: When the game window is not focused, the frame rate is capped (see Idle FPS Limit). When it is minimized, almost nothing is drawn (one frame a second) while the game keeps running. Playing in the focused window is never affected. No restart.
vesuvio.option.idleFpsLimit.tooltip: Frame rate while the window is open but not focused (3 to 60). The game itself keeps running at full speed. No restart.
vesuvio.option.hiddenWindowFps.tooltip: When the game window is hidden or completely covered (on macOS: Cmd+H, another Space or other windows over it all), almost nothing is drawn, as when it is minimized, while the game keeps running. Only works where the system tells the game; otherwise nothing changes. No restart.
vesuvio.option.pausedFps.tooltip: In single player, while the game is paused behind a menu (Esc, options), the frame rate is capped at Paused FPS Limit: the world stands still, so more frames only make heat and fan noise. No restart.
vesuvio.option.pausedFpsLimit.tooltip: Frame rate while single player is paused behind a menu (10 to 240). Default 60. No restart.
vesuvio.option.fastStartupCompile.toolti: macOS only: asks MoltenVK to let Metal compile shaders on more threads at once, so the short stutter when a new effect or block appears for the first time is shorter. No change in look. Needs a restart. Does nothing on Windows and Linux.
vesuvio.option.pipelineCache.tooltip: Saves the graphics driver's compiled shaders (Vulkan pipeline cache) in the vesuvio-cache folder when you quit, and gives them back at the next launch, so the game starts faster and the first sight of a new mob, effect or shader pass no longer hitches. The file is checked against the graphics card and driver and thrown away after a driver update. Biggest gain on Windows; on Mac Metal keeps its own cache, so the gain is smaller. No visual change. Needs a restart.
vesuvio.option.asyncSubmit.tooltip: macOS only: MoltenVK converts each frame to Metal on its own thread instead of the game's. Can raise FPS when the CPU is the limit; does nothing when the GPU is. Experimental: switch it off if you see flicker, stutter or crashes. No change in look. Needs a restart. Does nothing on Windows and Linux.
vesuvio.option.metalArgumentBuffersOff.t: macOS only, an experiment to measure: tells MoltenVK not to use Metal argument buffers, so the textures and buffers of each draw are bound one by one instead of through one table. The game makes a new table for almost every draw, so this may be faster or slower: run the Vesuvio benchmark with it off and on and keep whichever wins. Shader packs that use many textures at once (more than 16 in one shader) may fail to draw with it on; switch it off then. No change in look otherwise. Off by default. Needs a restart. Does nothing on Windows and Linux.
vesuvio.option.mergeTransferBarriers.too: After every copy to the graphics card (chunks, uniforms, entity and GUI vertices, textures) the game makes the GPU stop and wait until everything before it is finished. Copies that touch different memory do not need that, so back-to-back copies like these now share one wait, recorded before anything that could use their data. On Mac each wait also starts a new Metal command group, so loading chunks gets smoother. Same picture. No restart.
vesuvio.option.framebufferCache.tooltip: Every time the game starts drawing into a set of pictures it makes a Vulkan framebuffer (the list of those pictures) and throws it away after the frame, around 20 times a frame and many more with shader packs. Now each one is kept and reused while the same pictures are drawn into again, and thrown away when one of its pictures is (resizing the window, changing shader packs). A little less CPU time per frame. Same picture. No restart.
vesuvio.option.mappedVertexPools.tooltip: Only on computers whose graphics share the main memory (Apple silicon and other integrated GPUs; checked from what the driver reports): the vertices of mobs, block entities, particles and the GUI are written straight into the memory the graphics card draws them from, instead of into a staging buffer that the graphics card then copies over. Two to four GPU copies and waits less per frame. A buffer is only rewritten after the graphics card has finished every frame that used it. Same picture. Does nothing on other computers. No restart.
When the game looks for entities near a spot (mobs pushing each other, hoppers picking up items, mobs looking for targets), it checks only the few areas around that spot instead of walking a whole sorted list. Same entities, same order: no change in gameplay or looks. Works in single player and for your own player in multiplayer. No restart.
vesuvio.option.worldRareEntityIndex.tool: Only boats, minecarts, shulkers and happy ghasts can be bumped into, and only container minecarts and chest boats can feed a hopper. Each area keeps a short list of those, so moving mobs, dropped items and idle hoppers stop checking every cow and item around them. Same results as vanilla: no change in gameplay. Big help in mob farms and item collection areas. Needs a restart.
vesuvio.option.worldPathTypeCache.toolti: Mobs looking for a path ask "what kind of block is this" for hundreds of blocks; the answer only depends on the block, so it is worked out once per block type and remembered (forgotten again when data packs reload). Same paths as vanilla. Single player only (on a server the server does pathfinding). No restart.
vesuvio.option.worldPoiVerticalRange.too: Villagers looking for beds and workstations, bees looking for hives and golem spawning search a sphere around them, but vanilla reads every height of every chunk in it first. This reads only the heights the sphere reaches. Same results, same order: no change in gameplay. Single player only. No restart.
vesuvio.option.worldFastSuffocationCheck: Every mob checks each tick whether its head is inside a block. This does the same check without the extra objects vanilla creates for it. Same result: no change in gameplay. Single player only. No restart.
vesuvio.option.chunkScheduler.tooltip: Hands the chunk-building threads only as many sections per frame as they can work through, nearest to you first, instead of copying every changed section in view in one go. Removes the long frames when you join a world, teleport or fly into new terrain, and the threads always work on what is in front of you now. Sections you change and those within about 27 blocks are still built at once. Same picture: a waiting section keeps showing what it showed before and is built a few frames later. No restart.
vesuvio.option.skipEmptySections.tooltip: A 16x16x16 piece of the world that holds only air (most of the sky above the ground) gets its empty result straight away, without copying the world around it and without a building task. Vanilla builds every one of them, including again after each light change. Same picture. No restart.
vesuvio.option.trimSectionCopies.tooltip: To build a piece of the world the game copies it and its neighbours; each copy also took a copy of the whole chunk's list of chests, signs and other block entities. Now each copy keeps only its own. Less garbage and fewer memory pauses in bases full of storage. Same picture. No restart.
vesuvio.option.chunkUploadBudget.tooltip: Most milliseconds per frame spent sending finished chunks to the graphics card. Vanilla sends them all in the same frame, which can be tens of megabytes after a join or while flying: one long frame. With a budget the rest goes in the next frames; a chunk still appears only once it is complete, so you may see a new chunk a frame or two later, never half of one. If chunks keep waiting the budget grows by itself, and after 10 frames everything is sent at once. 0 = no limit (vanilla). Default 2. No restart.
vesuvio.option.mappedChunkStaging.toolti: Finished chunks are written straight into memory the graphics card can read, instead of being copied once more on the CPU before every upload. Uses up to about 150 MB more memory while on (the 98 MB vanilla staging area stays reserved but unused). Works together with the chunk upload budget. Same picture. No restart: takes effect the next time no chunk is waiting to be sent, usually within a frame.
vesuvio.option.translucentSortThrottle.t: See-through blocks (water, glass, ice) are sorted back to front again as you move. Vanilla does it on every block you walk for far sections lined up with you, e.g. a whole sea at your height. Now a far section is re-sorted once you have moved far enough for its order to change (every 2 blocks at 64 blocks away, every 8 at 256): the sort is never further off than vanilla allows for a section 32 blocks away. Nearby sections are sorted as in vanilla. Does nothing with Improved Transparency. No restart.
vesuvio.option.clearFusion.tooltip: When the game clears a picture (to a colour or to empty depth) and then draws into it, the clear now happens as the drawing starts instead of as a separate step that writes the whole picture out and reads it back in. Clears nothing can see (the GUI's depth clears) are skipped, and post effects stop making depth buffers they never read. Helps most with shader packs, menu blur and on Apple GPUs. The picture does not change. No restart.
